<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">Calibeating Made Simple</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Yurong Chen
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">

</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">We study calibeating, the problem of post-processing external forecasts online to minimize cumulative losses and match an informativeness-based benchmark.
Unlike prior work, which analyzed calibeating for specific losses with specific arguments, we reduce calibeating to existing online learning techniques and obtain results for general proper losses.
More concretely,
we first show that calibeating is minimax-equivalent to regret minimization.
This recovers the <math id="abstract1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(\log T)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(\log T)</annotation></semantics></math> calibeating rate of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx8" title="" class="ltx_ref">FH23</a>]</cite> for the Brier and log losses and its optimality,
and yields new optimal calibeating rates for mixable losses and general bounded losses.
Second, we prove that multi-calibeating is minimax-equivalent to the combination of calibeating and the classical expert problem.
This yields new optimal multi-calibeating rates for mixable losses, including Brier and log losses, and general bounded losses.
Finally, we obtain new bounds for achieving calibeating and calibration simultaneously for the Brier loss.
For binary predictions, our result gives the first calibrated algorithm that at the same time also achieves the optimal <math id="abstract1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(\log T)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(\log T)</annotation></semantics></math> calibeating rate.</p>
  
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Calibration has attracted growing attention in recent years as a desideratum for probabilistic prediction, motivated by the need to produce reliable probabilities for downstream decision-making <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Guo+17</a>]</cite>.
Despite its appeal as a benchmark for reliability,
however,
calibration is not necessarily a meaningful test of forecasting expertise.
For example, online calibration can be achieved
by randomized strategies
without any knowledge of the data-generating process <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx11" title="" class="ltx_ref">FV98</a>]</cite>.
Hence, calibration alone cannot distinguish true expertise from uninformative procedures.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To quantify and preserve forecasting expertise,
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx8" title="" class="ltx_ref">FH23</a>]</cite> introduced <em id="S1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">calibeating</em> in a post-processing setting. In this setting, an external forecaster (e.g., a machine learning model) outputs a probabilistic forecast at each round,
and then the learner produces its own forecast based on it.
It is known that for proper losses such as the Brier and log losses, the cumulative score can be decomposed into a calibration term, which measures the reliability, and a refinement term, which measures the informativeness and skill. This motivates the question of whether one can improve reliability without sacrificing skill.
Calibeating formalizes this goal by requiring the learner’s
loss to be as small as the external forecaster’s refinement score (in other words, to “beat”
the forecaster by its calibration error).</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Existing work <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx8" title="" class="ltx_ref">FH23</a>, <a href="#bib.bibx16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lee+22</a>]</cite> establishes online calibeating guarantees for
the Brier and log losses,
and studies extensions
such as
beating multiple forecasters (multi-calibeating) and imposing simultaneous calibration constraints. These results rely on loss-specialized
analyses. More broadly, the fundamental statistical difficulty of calibeating and its relationship to standard online-learning problems have remained unclear, leaving open whether known bounds are optimal or how they
generalize beyond the Brier and log losses.</p>
</div>
<section id="S1.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">1.1 </span>Our Results</h3>

<div id="S1.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We study calibeating from an online-learning perspective. Rather than analyzing different losses on a case-by-case basis, we identify simple reductions from (multi-)calibeating to standard online-learning primitives.
This yields a “plug-and-play” analysis:
by instantiating the reductions with classical online-learning algorithms, we obtain general upper and lower bounds in a modular way.</p>
</div>
<section id="S1.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Calibeating <math id="S1.SS1.SSS0.Px1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="=" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>=</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">=</annotation></semantics></math> no-regret learning (<a href="#S3" title="3 Calibeating = No-Regret Learning ‣ Calibeating Made Simple" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>).</h4>

<div id="S1.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We prove that calibeating is minimax-equivalent to regret minimization.
<a href="#S3.Thmtheorem1" title="Theorem 3.1. ‣ 3 Calibeating = No-Regret Learning ‣ Calibeating Made Simple" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Theorem</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a> gives a reduction that turns any no-regret learner with regret bound <math id="S1.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha(T)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>T</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha(T)</annotation></semantics></math> into a calibeating algorithm with a corresponding bound that scales with <math id="S1.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|Q|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>Q</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|Q|</annotation></semantics></math>, the number of distinct
external forecast values over <math id="S1.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math> rounds.
The reduction exploits the fact that the refinement benchmark decomposes across distinct forecast values, allowing one to treat each corresponding subsequence independently.
Instantiating this reduction recovers the <math id="S1.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(|Q|\log T)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>Q</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(|Q|\log T)</annotation></semantics></math> guarantees for the Brier and log losses from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx8" title="" class="ltx_ref">FH23</a>]</cite> and extends them to general mixable losses (<a href="#S3.Thmtheorem4" title="Corollary 3.4. ‣ 3 Calibeating = No-Regret Learning ‣ Calibeating Made Simple" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Corollary</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.4</span></a>).
We also obtain an <math id="S1.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(\sqrt{|Q|T})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msqrt><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>Q</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow></msqrt><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(\sqrt{|Q|T})</annotation></semantics></math> bound for general bounded proper losses (<a href="#S3.Thmtheorem2" title="Corollary 3.2. ‣ 3 Calibeating = No-Regret Learning ‣ Calibeating Made Simple" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Corollary</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a>).
Conversely, <a href="#S3.Thmtheorem5" title="Theorem 3.5. ‣ 3 Calibeating = No-Regret Learning ‣ Calibeating Made Simple" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Theorem</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.5</span></a> provides a matching lower bound that completes the minimax-equivalence.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S1.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Multi-calibeating <math id="S1.SS1.SSS0.Px2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="=" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>=</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">=</annotation></semantics></math> calibeating <math id="S1.SS1.SSS0.Px2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>+</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+</annotation></semantics></math> expert problem (<a href="#S4" title="4 Multi-Calibeating = Calibeating + Expert Problem ‣ Calibeating Made Simple" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>).</h4>

<div id="S1.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Next, we present (in <a href="#S4.Thmtheorem1" title="Theorem 4.1. ‣ Expert Problem. ‣ 4 Multi-Calibeating = Calibeating + Expert Problem ‣ Calibeating Made Simple" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Theorem</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.1</span></a>) a simple decomposition of multi-calibeating into calibeating and the expert problem:
run a separate calibeating subroutine for each forecaster to produce candidate predictions, then aggregate them with an expert algorithm.
The resulting multi-calibeating guarantee is the sum of the calibeating bound and the expert regret bound.
For mixable losses,
we obtain a logarithmic bound of
<math id="S1.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(\log N+|Q^{(n)}|\log T)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msup><mi>Q</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(\log N+|Q^{(n)}|\log T)</annotation></semantics></math> (<a href="#S4.Thmtheorem3" title="Corollary 4.3. ‣ Expert Problem. ‣ 4 Multi-Calibeating = Calibeating + Expert Problem ‣ Calibeating Made Simple" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Corollary</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.3</span></a>), where <math id="S1.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> is the number of forecasters and <math id="S1.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Q^{(n)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>Q</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q^{(n)}</annotation></semantics></math> is the set of distinct forecasts produced by forecaster <math id="S1.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math>.
This improves exponentially over the polynomial dependence on <math id="S1.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx8" title="" class="ltx_ref">FH23</a>]</cite> and the polynomial dependence on <math id="S1.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math> in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lee+22</a>]</cite>.
We complement this with a lower-bound reduction (<a href="#S4.Thmtheorem4" title="Theorem 4.4. ‣ Expert Problem. ‣ 4 Multi-Calibeating = Calibeating + Expert Problem ‣ Calibeating Made Simple" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Theorem</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.4</span></a>), showing that multi-calibeating inherits hardness from both the expert problem and the calibeating problem.
This yields matching lower bounds for Brier and log losses and shows the tightness of our results (<a href="#S4.Thmtheorem6" title="Corollary 4.6. ‣ Expert Problem. ‣ 4 Multi-Calibeating = Calibeating + Expert Problem ‣ Calibeating Made Simple" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Corollary</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.6</span></a>).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S1.SS1.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Simultaneous (multi-)calibeating and calibration for Brier loss (<a href="#S5" title="5 Calibeating and Calibration at the Same Time ‣ Calibeating Made Simple" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>).</h4>

<div id="S1.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Finally, we provide new bounds for achieving calibeating and calibration simultaneously.
We propose a meta-algorithm that tracks an arbitrary reference
algorithm
while ensuring calibration (<a href="#S5.Thmtheorem1" title="Theorem 5.1. ‣ 5 Calibeating and Calibration at the Same Time ‣ Calibeating Made Simple" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Theorem</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.1</span></a>).
The construction employs two existing online learning primitives:
the reduction by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx2" title="" class="ltx_ref">BM07</a>]</cite> to enforce calibration via the calibration-swap-regret connection, and a two-expert algorithm by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx22" title="" class="ltx_ref">SNL14</a>]</cite> to aggregate the predictions from the  <span title="" class="ltx_glossaryref ltx_missing">BM</span> (<abbr title="" class="ltx_glossaryref ltx_missing">BM</abbr>) reduction and the reference algorithm.
Instantiating the reference with the (multi-)calibeating algorithms from the previous sections, for the Brier loss, we obtain for the binary case the optimal logarithmic (multi-)calibeating rate of <math id="S1.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(\log N+|Q^{(n)}|\log T)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msup><mi>Q</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(\log N+|Q^{(n)}|\log T)</annotation></semantics></math>
while ensuring a sublinear <math id="S1.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell_{2}</annotation></semantics></math>-calibration error of
order
<math id="S1.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{O}(\sqrt{T})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>O</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msqrt><mi>T</mi></msqrt><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{O}(\sqrt{T})</annotation></semantics></math> (<a href="#S5.Thmtheorem2" title="Corollary 5.2. ‣ 5 Calibeating and Calibration at the Same Time ‣ Calibeating Made Simple" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Corollary</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.2</span></a>).
This improves the polynomial <math id="S1.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math>-dependence on the calibeating side
in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx8" title="" class="ltx_ref">FH23</a>]</cite> and improves both sides compared to <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lee+22</a>]</cite>.
For multi-class outcomes, we derive explicit tradeoffs between (multi-)calibeating and calibration (<a href="#S5.Thmtheorem3" title="Corollary 5.3. ‣ 5 Calibeating and Calibration at the Same Time ‣ Calibeating Made Simple" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Corollary</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.3</span></a>). In particular, at one extreme, we recover the known dependence on <math id="S1.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math> for calibration <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx8" title="" class="ltx_ref">FH23</a>, <a href="#bib.bibx9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fis+25</a>]</cite> while dropping the <math id="S1.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|Q^{(n)}|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msup><mi>Q</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|Q^{(n)}|</annotation></semantics></math> dependence in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx8" title="" class="ltx_ref">FH23</a>]</cite>.
For a summary of our results and comparisons with prior work, see <a href="#S1.T1" title="In Simultaneous (multi-)calibeating and calibration for Brier loss (). ‣ 1.1 Our Results ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Calibeating Made Simple" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.T1" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 1: </span>Comparison of prior and our guarantees in <math id="S1.T1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S1.T1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S1.T1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> (the number of outcomes), and <math id="S1.T1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|Q|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>Q</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|Q|</annotation></semantics></math> (we assume <math id="S1.T1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|Q^{(n)}|=|Q|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msup><mi>Q</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>Q</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|Q^{(n)}|=|Q|</annotation></semantics></math> for simplicity). For simultaneous calibeating and calibration, the first rate is for calibeating and the second for calibration. We omit polynomial dependence on <math id="S1.T1.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> for presentation clarity, and <math id="S1.T1.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{O}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>O</mi><mo mathsize="1.110em">~</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{O}</annotation></semantics></math> omits logarithmic dependence on <math id="S1.T1.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math>.
The simultaneous results of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx8" title="" class="ltx_ref">FH23</a>]</cite> are only for calibeating (but not multi-calibeating), so we only show results for calibeating for comparison.
The results of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lee+22</a>]</cite> are only for binary outcomes. </figcaption>

<td id="S1.T1.19.1.11.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top"></td>

</section>
<section id="S1.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">1.2 </span>Related Work</h3>

<section id="S1.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Calibeating.</h4>

<div id="S1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In the seminal work proposing calibeating, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx8" title="" class="ltx_ref">FH23</a>]</cite> give online guarantees for the Brier and log losses via a bin-wise estimation viewpoint. They also study extensions to multiple forecasters and to simultaneous calibeating and calibration.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lee+22</a>]</cite> formulate simultaneous multi-calibration and multi-calibeating as an online multi-objective optimization problem, achieving favorable dependence on the number of external forecasters but suboptimal dependence on the time horizon.
In comparison, our results are obtained via reductions that connect calibeating to standard online-learning problems.
Finally, as an application, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx12" title="" class="ltx_ref">GR23</a>]</cite> apply calibeating as a robustness layer on top of online Platt scaling to guarantee adversarial calibration in binary classification while preserving predictive performance.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S1.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Online recalibration.</h4>

<div id="S1.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Online recalibration is studied in the same post-processing setting as calibeating, but it benchmarks performance by proper-loss regret rather than refinement.
The goal is to achieve small regret relative to the external forecaster while simultaneously ensuring calibrated predictions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx19" title="" class="ltx_ref">MKE25</a>, <a href="#bib.bibx7" title="" class="ltx_ref">DMK24</a>]</cite>.
For binary classification, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx15" title="" class="ltx_ref">KE17</a>]</cite> provide adversarial online guarantees, and <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx20" title="" class="ltx_ref">OKS24</a>]</cite> obtain improved bounds and explicit regret versus <math id="S1.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell_{1}</annotation></semantics></math>-calibration tradeoffs via Blackwell approachability for
strictly proper losses.
These tradeoffs yield sublinear but typically polynomial-in-<math id="S1.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math> rates. While we focus on the Brier loss in our simultaneous guarantee, we target the stronger refinement benchmark and achieve logarithmic-in-<math id="S1.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math> rates while still ensuring sublinear <math id="S1.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell_{2}</annotation></semantics></math>-calibration.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S1.SS2.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Calibration and proper scoring loss.</h4>

<div id="S1.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Proper scoring losses admit classical decompositions into a reliability (calibration) term and an informativeness (refinement) term <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Daw06</a>, <a href="#bib.bibx21" title="" class="ltx_ref">San63</a>, <a href="#bib.bibx3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Brö09</a>]</cite>. In this spirit, <math id="S1.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell_{2}</annotation></semantics></math>-calibration <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx11" title="" class="ltx_ref">FV98</a>]</cite> and KL-calibration <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx18" title="" class="ltx_ref">LSS25</a>]</cite> can be viewed as online analogues of the calibration term for the Brier loss and the log loss, respectively; more generally, this motivates defining online calibration measures compatible with arbitrary proper scoring losses.
Several calibration notions, including <math id="S1.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell_{2}</annotation></semantics></math>-calibration <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fis+25</a>]</cite> and KL-calibration <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx18" title="" class="ltx_ref">LSS25</a>]</cite>, have been shown to be equivalent to swap-regret objectives.
We exploit this connection in our simultaneous guarantees by enforcing (pseudo-)swap regret via the <abbr title="" class="ltx_glossaryref ltx_missing">BM</abbr> reduction <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx2" title="" class="ltx_ref">BM07</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Model</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We consider an online prediction problem over a finite outcome space with <math id="S2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> external forecasts.
Let <math id="S2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K\geq 2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K\geq 2</annotation></semantics></math> be the number of possible outcomes, and <math id="S2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta_{K}\coloneqq\{p\in\mathbb{R}^{K}_{\geq 0}:\sum^{K}_{k=1}p_{k}=1\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mo>≔</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>∈</mo><msubsup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≥</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mi>K</mi></msubsup></mrow><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.111em">:</mo><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>K</mi></msubsup><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta_{K}\coloneqq\{p\in\mathbb{R}^{K}_{\geq 0}:\sum^{K}_{k=1}p_{k}=1\}</annotation></semantics></math> be the probability simplex.
We let <math id="S2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[n]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[n]</annotation></semantics></math> denote the set <math id="S2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{1,\dots,n\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{1,\dots,n\}</annotation></semantics></math> for any positive integer <math id="S2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math>.
The outcome space is denoted by <math id="S2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{E}\coloneqq\{e_{i}:i\in[K]\}\subseteq\Delta_{K}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><mo>≔</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>e</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>K</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mo>⊆</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>K</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{E}\coloneqq\{e_{i}:i\in[K]\}\subseteq\Delta_{K}</annotation></semantics></math>,
where <math id="S2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>e</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> is the <math id="S2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>-th standard basis vector.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The interaction proceeds for <math id="S2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math> rounds. At each round <math id="S2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t\in[T]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>T</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t\in[T]</annotation></semantics></math>, the learner first observes <math id="S2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> external forecasts, <math id="S2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q^{(n)}_{t}\in\Delta_{K}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>q</mi><mi>t</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>K</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q^{(n)}_{t}\in\Delta_{K}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n\in[N]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>N</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n\in[N]</annotation></semantics></math>, and makes its own prediction <math id="S2.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{t}\in\Delta_{K}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>K</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{t}\in\Delta_{K}</annotation></semantics></math>. The outcome <math id="S2.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y_{t}\in\mathcal{E}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y_{t}\in\mathcal{E}</annotation></semantics></math> is then revealed, and the learner incurs loss <math id="S2.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell(p_{t},y_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell(p_{t},y_{t})</annotation></semantics></math>.
For simplicity, we assume that <math id="S2.p2.m9" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="q_{1:T}\coloneqq(q_{t})^{T}_{t=1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow></msub><mo>≔</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>T</mi></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q_{1:T}\coloneqq(q_{t})^{T}_{t=1}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.p2.m10" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="y_{1:T}\coloneqq(y_{t})^{T}_{t=1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow></msub><mo>≔</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>T</mi></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y_{1:T}\coloneqq(y_{t})^{T}_{t=1}</annotation></semantics></math> are generated by an oblivious adversary, i.e., they are decided at time <math id="S2.p2.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t=0</annotation></semantics></math> with complete knowledge of the learner’s algorithm (but not its random bits).</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Throughout, we consider a proper scoring loss
<math id="S2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell:\Delta_{K}\times\mathcal{E}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>ℝ</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell:\Delta_{K}\times\mathcal{E}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}</annotation></semantics></math>, i.e., losses such that
for any <math id="S2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q\in\Delta_{K}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>K</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q\in\Delta_{K}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q\in\arg\min_{p\in\Delta_{K}}\mathbb{E}_{y\sim q}[\ell(p,y)]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>arg</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msub><mi>min</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>K</mi></msub></mrow></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>∼</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q\in\arg\min_{p\in\Delta_{K}}\mathbb{E}_{y\sim q}[\ell(p,y)]</annotation></semantics></math>.
We write <math id="S2.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell(p,q)\coloneqq\mathbb{E}_{y\sim q}[\ell(p,y)]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≔</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>∼</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell(p,q)\coloneqq\mathbb{E}_{y\sim q}[\ell(p,y)]</annotation></semantics></math>.
Let <math id="S2.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{1}\{\cdot\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>𝟏</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{1}\{\cdot\}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the indicator function, which equals one if the condition holds and zero otherwise.
Given a prediction sequence <math id="S2.p3.m6" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="p_{1:T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{1:T}</annotation></semantics></math> and outcome sequence <math id="S2.p3.m7" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="y_{1:T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y_{1:T}</annotation></semantics></math>, for any <math id="S2.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p\in\Delta_{K}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>K</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p\in\Delta_{K}</annotation></semantics></math>, denote the number of times the learner predicts <math id="S2.p3.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math> as <math id="S2.p3.m10" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="n_{T}(p)\coloneqq\sum^{T}_{t=1}\mathbf{1}\{p_{t}=p\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.111em">≔</mo><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>T</mi></msubsup><mn>𝟏</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n_{T}(p)\coloneqq\sum^{T}_{t=1}\mathbf{1}\{p_{t}=p\}</annotation></semantics></math>,
and the empirical outcome distribution conditioned on prediction <math id="S2.p3.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math> as <math id="S2.p3.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho^{p}_{T}(y)\coloneqq\frac{1}{n_{T}(p)}\sum^{T}_{t=1}\mathbf{1}\{p_{t}=p,y_{t}=y\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>ρ</mi><mi>T</mi><mi>p</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≔</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>T</mi></msubsup><mrow><mn>𝟏</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho^{p}_{T}(y)\coloneqq\frac{1}{n_{T}(p)}\sum^{T}_{t=1}\mathbf{1}\{p_{t}=p,y_{t}=y\}</annotation></semantics></math> for <math id="S2.p3.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y\in\mathcal{E}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y\in\mathcal{E}</annotation></semantics></math>, whenever <math id="S2.p3.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n_{T}(p)&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n_{T}(p)&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math>.
With these definitions, the cumulative loss, refinement score, and calibration error are defined as follows.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.Thmtheorem1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_definition">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="S2.Thmtheorem1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Definition 2.1</span></span><span id="S2.Thmtheorem1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The <em id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">cumulative loss</em> of predictions <math id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="p_{1:T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{1:T}</annotation></semantics></math> under outcomes <math id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="y_{1:T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y_{1:T}</annotation></semantics></math> is</p>

<p id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">The <em id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1.2.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">refinement score</em> is</p>

<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.Ex2.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\displaystyle R_{T}(p_{1:T},y_{1:T})\coloneqq\sum_{p}n_{T}(p)\ell(\rho^{p}_{T},\rho^{p}_{T})=\sum_{p}\min_{q\in\Delta_{K}}\sum_{t:p_{t}=p}\ell(q,y_{t})~." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>≔</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><munder><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mi>p</mi></munder></mstyle><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>ρ</mi><mi>T</mi><mi>p</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>ρ</mi><mi>T</mi><mi>p</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><munder><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mi>p</mi></munder></mstyle><munder><mi>min</mi><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>K</mi></msub></mrow></munder><mstyle displaystyle="true"><munder><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></mrow></munder></mstyle><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo rspace="0.052em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle R_{T}(p_{1:T},y_{1:T})\coloneqq\sum_{p}n_{T}(p)\ell(\rho^{p}_{T},\rho^{p}_{T})=\sum_{p}\min_{q\in\Delta_{K}}\sum_{t:p_{t}=p}\ell(q,y_{t})~.</annotation></semantics></math></td>

<p id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1.3" class="ltx_p">Finally, the <em id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1.3.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">calibration error</em> is</p>
<table id="S2.EGx3" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.Ex3.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\displaystyle K_{T}(p_{1:T},y_{1:T})\coloneqq L_{T}(p_{1:T},y_{1:T})-R_{T}(p_{1:T},y_{1:T})~." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>≔</mo><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow></msub><mo rspace="0.052em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle K_{T}(p_{1:T},y_{1:T})\coloneqq L_{T}(p_{1:T},y_{1:T})-R_{T}(p_{1:T},y_{1:T})~.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">By construction, <math id="S2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L_{T}=R_{T}+K_{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>K</mi><mi>T</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L_{T}=R_{T}+K_{T}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K_{T}\geq 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo>≥</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K_{T}\geq 0</annotation></semantics></math>.
Moreover,
<math id="S2.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K_{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>K</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K_{T}</annotation></semantics></math> coincides with the full-swap-regret notion of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fis+25</a>]</cite>, while
<math id="S2.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{T}</annotation></semantics></math> corresponds to the best-in-hindsight swap-regret benchmark. Indeed, for each prediction <math id="S2.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math>, the refinement term equals the loss of the best constant predictor over rounds with <math id="S2.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{t}=p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{t}=p</annotation></semantics></math>. Thus, the refinement score measures the informativeness of the forecasts: sequences that induce finer bins with lower within-bin variability achieve smaller refinement. In contrast, the calibration error measures within-bin reliability, i.e., how close the issued prediction <math id="S2.p4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math> is to the empirical conditional distribution <math id="S2.p4.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho^{p}_{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>ρ</mi><mi>T</mi><mi>p</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho^{p}_{T}</annotation></semantics></math> on the corresponding subsequence.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Proper scoring losses admit a classic decomposition into terms measuring the
informativeness (or refinement) of forecasts and their reliability (or calibration)
in a probabilistic setting; see, e.g., <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Brö09</a>, <a href="#bib.bibx6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Daw06</a>]</cite>.
<a href="#S2.Thmtheorem1" title="Definition 2.1. ‣ 2 Model ‣ Calibeating Made Simple" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Definition</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.1</span></a> can be seen as the empirical counterparts of these quantities.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.Thmtheorem2" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_example">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="S2.Thmtheorem2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Example 2.2</span></span><span id="S2.Thmtheorem2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="S2.Thmtheorem2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.Thmtheorem2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For <em id="S2.Thmtheorem2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Brier loss</em> <math id="S2.Thmtheorem2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell(p,y)=\|p-y\|^{2}_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell(p,y)=\|p-y\|^{2}_{2}</annotation></semantics></math>,
the refinement score equals the weighted sum of within-bin variances, and the calibration error becomes the
<math id="S2.Thmtheorem2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell_{2}</annotation></semantics></math>-calibration <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx11" title="" class="ltx_ref">FV98</a>]</cite>,</p>
<table id="S2.EGx4" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S2.Ex4"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.Ex4.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\displaystyle lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><munder><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mi>p</mi></munder></mstyle><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∥</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>−</mo><msubsup><mi>ρ</mi><mi>T</mi><mi>p</mi></msubsup><msubsup><mo
